The Common triplefin Forsterygion lapillum is a small benthic fish endemic to New Zealand's rocky shores. In the waters around White Islands during 2017, field surveys recorded the maximum gonadosomatic index (GSI) for females at 28% [GSI = 28%] at a water temperature of 19.8 °C [T = 19.8 °C]. The early life stages of this species are marked by a rapid developmental schedule. At 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the pelagic egg stage lasts only about 14 days  before eclosion occurs, and the newly emerged prolarva has a total length at hatch of merely 0.49 centimeters . The time since hatching at birth is essentially negligible, recorded as just 1 day , reflecting the immediate transition from the yolk-sac to the onset of active feeding at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C].

The planktonic larval phase in Forsterygion lapillum is characterized by considerable somatic growth before the dramatic morphological shift of metamorphosis. At a mean ambient temperature of 19.8 °C [T = 19.8 °C], the time since hatching at metamorphosis is approximately 52 days , a period during which the free-swimming larva attains a total length at metamorphosis of 2.78 centimeters . The wet weight at metamorphosis, derived from length-weight relationships for post-flexion individuals, is approximately 0.1831 grams , marking a substantial increase from the hatchling stage. This transition is a critical bottleneck for survival, as the pelagic larva must successfully settle to the benthos and undergo the body plan reorganization necessary for a demersal lifestyle. The relatively precise timing of this event under stable thermal conditions underscores its dependence on environmental temperature for physiological rate control.

Following settlement, the post-metamorphic juvenile enters a period of rapid mass gain and sexual maturation. The von Bertalanffy growth rate for this species has been estimated at 0.0033 per day  when studied at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a growth coefficient that reflects the species' moderately fast life history. The time since hatching at puberty is 270 days [tp = 270 days] at 19.8 °C [T = 19.8 °C], and at this point individuals typically measure about 5 centimeters [Lp = about 5 centimeters] in total length at puberty. The corresponding wet weight at puberty reaches about 1.2052 grams [Wwp = about 1.2052 grams], representing a considerable energetic investment in somatic tissue before the first allocation of resources to gamete production. This linear size at maturity appears consistent with the constraints imposed by the need to acquire and defend a small territory on the shallow subtidal reef.

The ultimate size of Forsterygion lapillum is modest compared to many other tripterygiids. The maximum recorded total length, or ultimate total length, in local populations reaches 8 centimeters [Li = 8 centimeters], with most adults ranging from 4 to 8 centimeters in total length. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to this maximum size is 5.4586 grams [Wwi = 5.4586 grams], a value derived from established length-mass regressions for the species. The documented maximum lifespan from field mark-recapture studies is 730 days [am = 730 days] at 19.8 °C [T = 19.8 °C], making the Common triplefin a relatively short-lived species typical of small-bodied, high-turnover rocky reef fishes. This lifespan constraint, coupled with the moderate growth coefficient, suggests that individuals must channel energy efficiently into both growth and reproduction within a narrow temporal window to maximize lifetime fitness.

The overall life history of the Common triplefin is typical of a small, iteroparous reef fish with a high adult mortality rate. The birth mass of a newly hatched larva is exceedingly small, calculated from an egg diameter of roughly 1.12 millimeters to be just 0.000736 grams [Wwb = 0.000736 grams] at the moment of chorion rupture. This tiny size underscores the vulnerability of the planktonic stage to starvation and predation. The peak gonadosomatic index of 28% [GSI = 28%] was recorded during the summer spawning peak at a temperature of 19.8 °C [T = 19.8 °C]. A comparative view of this species' life history reveals a strategy of early maturation and rapid growth, a pattern that aligns well with that of other small triplefins occupying similar intertidal and subtidal niches along New Zealand's temperate coastline.
